nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Code Goby
Scientific Name:  Gobiosoma robustum

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Gobiidae

Other Common Names:  robust goby

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: No known commercial value.
Recreational: No known recreational value.
Ecological role: Small predator comprising one of the dominant species of shallow grass flats (303 326 515 664 786 788).  This goby was sixth in percent occurrence in a seagrass study by Gilmore (993) being present in 53% of the samples taken. It ranked 16th in abundance in the same study. Indicator: No information available.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall: Martha's Vineyard to Florida and throughout the Gulf of Mexico to the Yucatan (56 237 327 632 788 891 1037).  Abundant in shallow sea grass meadows especially in Florida and northern Gulf of Mexico (237 303 664).  Considered a year round resident of seagrass beds (786) with no reported migratory behavior.  Some movements associated with temperature fluctuations have been observed (349 391).  Studies in Florida report movement to shore during coldest months, and then back to bays as temperatures increase (378 581).

Within Study Area: Extremely common along Gulf coast from southern Texas to Key West Florida in shallow grass flats (56 237 303 664 786).  Abundant in seagrass beds throughout the Indian River Lagoon system (1136 1009 993 1233 1187 1243 1183).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Demersal/epibenthic euryhaline predator (26 58 170 261 378 581 664 703 786 515).  Reported seasonal abundance patterns are unclear and often in conflict possibly due to the difficulty in trapping this cryptic species (664 326 786 391).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Egg:  Habitat preferences of early life stages are unknown; eggs have been found attached to shells or sponges (68).
Juveniles: Juveniles and adults have a strong affinity for drift algae associated with seagrass (Schooley 1977; 1170 2352)
Adults: Adults are primarily collected from oligohaline to euhaline estuaries in shallow water sea grasses particularly Thallasia, but also in Diplanthera, Ruppia, Halodule, and Cymodocea grass beds (664 1116).  Adults are also found in bays, beach ponds, oyster reefs, river sloughs, rocky channels, and mangrove roots (68 26 303 378 664 667 702 703 326 322 786 58 327 349 724).

Other: Uncommon in deeper waters, with most collections occurring at depths of a few centimeters to 6.1 m (68 581 664 667 349).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body: Adults: Adults primarily collected over muddy bottoms of grass beds, but also occur in sponge beds, scallop beds, oyster shell, over bottoms of sand, and mud with shell (26 68 349 378 702 703 786 1116 1155).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Egg:  Egg Development has been observed from 15.5 to 18.5 C (68).
Larvae:  Larvae collected in Old Tampa Bay when mean temperatures at sampling stations ranged from 22.1 to 29.5 C (1341).  In Laguna de Terminos, Mexico, larvae were more abundant in the cool months (Dec. to Feb.) with temperatures between 25 and 28 C (2353).
Adult:   Collected over a range of 10.0 to 38.9 C (26 58 170 581 664 2350).  Peak abundance has been reported to occur at an average temperature of 23 C (58 391).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Larvae:  Larvae collected in Old Tampa Bay when mean salinities at sampling stations ranged from 21.6 ppt to 24.6 ppt (1341). In Laguna de Terminos, Mexico, larvae were more abundant in salinities from 25 to 30 ppt (2353).
Adult:   Collected over a wide salinity range, occur from 0 to 37.6 ppt, but are reported to prefer intermediate to moderately high salinities ranging predominately from 22 to 32 ppt (26 58 170 261 378 581 664 703 953).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Code gobies are gonochoristic, oviparous, and sexually dimorphic. The attached dermersal eggs are probably fertilized externally and may be defended by the male (68 905)
Mating/Spawning: Spawning occurs from early spring to late summer and from late summer through early fall in Tampa Bay (667).  Ripe females have been collected in the fall and winter months in Tampa Bay (664).  Young occur in Mississippi waters from July through September or October (170).  Spawning has been observed throughout the year in the study area particularly during late spring and early summer with a peak reported in May (170 185 349).  In Laguna de Terminos, Mexico, spawning occurs throughout the year (2353).  Variations in spawning behavior are possibly due to the different temperature patterns found throughout the range of this species (170 185).  Temperatures greater than 19 C have been reported as necessary for spawning to occur, but at temperatures greater than 30 C spawning slows down or ceases altogether in Florida populations (667 185). Spawning occurs during falling salinities (<45 ppt) in Texas (185) and from 19.2 to 23.0 ppt in Florida populations (667).
Fecundity: Both left and right ovaries ripen equally with approximately equal numbers of eggs; a 27 mm SL female was reported with 349 eggs in its right ovary, and 346 eggs in its left.  Number of eggs produced appears to be related to the size of the female with 56 per ovary observed in a 15 mm SL fish and 397 per ovary observed in a 28 mm SL fish.  Eggs are apparently spawned in toto, but two spawnings per season are considered possible (667).

nodes.title: Development
nodes.body:
Egg: Ovarian eggs are transparent until a diameter of .102 - .136 mm is attained and then they become more opaque.  Eggs are ripe at .476 - .782 mm (667).  Fertilized eggs are elliptical, opaque, slightly yellowish with a clear envelope; length varies from 1.30 - 1.40 mm in June to 1.55 - 1.70 mm in March, while width varies from 0.50 mm in June to 0.60 - 0.70 mm in March (68).  Eggs are attached by filaments attached to the chorion at the germinal end, and have an opaque, slightly yellowish yolk with a widely variable number of oil droplets scattered over its surface (68 667).  In eggs of unknown age collected on March 14, the head was large and prominent 22.25 h after collection; after another 26.25 h, the embryo formed; somites were visible after another 41.25 h; heart was visible and beating after another 27.5 h.  Total observation period covered 117.25 h with embryos dying before hatching (68).
Larvae: Larvae are planktonic and range in size from 1.9 to 9.6 mm TL.  They are present throughout the year in Laguna de Terminos, Mexico and are most abundant in salinities between 25 and 30 ppt during the winter months (Zavala et al. 1989).
Juvenile: Described specimens are 5.6 to 8.78 mm SL (667).  All fin elements present by 5.6 - 8.5 mm SL (667).  Increase in pigmentation, appearance of tubular nostrils and a series of rows of papillae on lower jaw, forehead, and cheeks by 8.78 mm SL.  Growth rate is moderate with 0_class fish reaching 28.4 to 29.0 mm TL by the end of their first year (170 664).
Adult: Minimum sizes noted for sexually mature adults were 13.1 mm TL(170) and 14.6 mm SL for females when only a few months old (667), and 16.5 mm TL for males (68).  Sex ratios are usually 1:1 (667).  Robins et al (788) suggested that the species attains a size of 50mm.  Maximum reported sizes are 31.5 mm TL for females (170), and 44 mm SL for males (667). Males are usually larger on the average than females (667).  Maximum reported size for this species is 55.5 mm TL or 45.0 mm SL for an unsexed fish (237).  Considered an annual fish with few, if any, individuals living over one year, although some males may live up to 2 years (667).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Code gobies are small benthic predators feeding principally on amphipods, mysids, chironomid larvae, decapod shrimp, molluscs, copepods, isopods, gamarids, cladocerans, ostracods, small molluscs, and some algal filaments and detritus when 15 to 35 mm SL (515 581 664).  Smaller individuals, 7 - 15 mm SL, were found to have eaten harpacticoid copepods, juvenile mysids, cumaceans, and many pennate diatoms (515).  Huh and Kitting (1985) found code gobies, 6-20 mm SL, were carnivorous during all seasons eating a variable mixture of amphipods, polychaetes, and copepods, while those over 20 mm SL ate primarily amphipods (<60% dry weight) throughout the year.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Code gobies are found in association with Orthopristis chrysopteris, Syngnathus scovelli, and Syngnathus floridae (303).  Reported predators include Synodus foetens, Cynoscion nebulosus, and Lutjanus griseus (664 672 700 702 724).
